finding: Does an individual owner (not a corporation) have to report?
verified_value: Yes. Sec. 37.15(a) requires 'owners of residential dwelling units' to report. No entity-type or portfolio-size exemption appears in the text.

finding: Is there a licence application to file or an approval to wait for?
verified_value: No application. The licence is generated automatically once the unit is reported as non-owner-occupied in the Housing Inventory.
note: Widely repeated online claims of a licence 'application' are not supported by the official page.

finding: Must the licence exist before the increase takes effect?
verified_value: Yes. A current rent increase licence must be on file before any annual or banked increase goes into effect; without it the notice is not enforceable.

finding: What happens if the owner has not reported?
verified_value: The licence is suspended. On reporting, it is restored prospectively only; the tenant is not obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the suspension.
note: Sec. 37.15(e). This is not retroactive - late reporting does not revive past months.

finding: When did reporting start for a building of this size?
verified_value: March 1, 2023 for condominiums and buildings with fewer than 10 units. July 1, 2022 applied only to non-condo buildings with 10 or more units.

finding: Annual reporting deadline
verified_value: March 1 each year.

finding: Penalty for reporting after the deadline
verified_value: The Rent Board does not assess monetary penalties for late Housing Inventory filing. A submission after the deadline still generates a licence.

finding: Must the licence be attached to the rent increase notice?
verified_value: No. The licence does not need to be included with the notice.

finding: Cost and method of reporting
verified_value: Free, online through the Rent Board Portal, available 24/7. An account is required.

finding: Is the submitted inventory information confidential?
verified_value: No. Information entered in the Housing Inventory submission is public.
note: Privacy consequence: do not put tenant names in free-text fields; the portal asks for owner business contact details, occupancy dates and base rent in $250 increments.

finding: Is a Rent Board petition needed for an annual or banked increase?
verified_value: No. Annual and banked increases do not require a petition or Board approval. The Rent Board lists six increase types that require a petition filed before the notice, and an annual or banked increase is not one of them.

finding: Rent Board fee (separate from the Inventory)
verified_value: $59.00 per dwelling unit for the 2026-2027 tax year, due March 1. 5% monthly late penalty, capped at 15%.

finding: Does a fee exemption satisfy the Inventory requirement?
verified_value: No. Requesting a Rent Board fee exemption does not satisfy Housing Inventory reporting.

finding: Has this owner actually reported / is a licence on file?
note: Cannot be checked without the property address and portal access. Tenants can look this up in the public portal. This is the first action item.

finding: Allowable annual increase, 3/1/2026 - 2/28/2027
How the annual figure is set
verified_value: 60% of the published CPI increase; in no event greater than 7%.

finding: How often rent may be increased
verified_value: Once every 12 months per tenancy.

finding: First possible increase
verified_value: 12 months after the date the tenant's lease began.

finding: What the percentage applies to
verified_value: Base rent only, including housing services such as parking or storage. Temporary passthroughs and fluctuating charges are excluded.

finding: Rounding
verified_value: Increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar.

finding: Which year's percentage to use
verified_value: The percentage in effect on the effective date of the increase, not the date the notice is served.

finding: Allowable increase, 3/1/2027 - 2/29/2028
note: Not yet published. The Rent Board publishes it on March 1, 2027. Left blank deliberately.

finding: Initial rent for a genuinely new vacant tenancy
verified_value: No limit under the Rent Ordinance on the first rent charged for an empty covered unit.

finding: Ordinance text on banking
verified_value: Sec. 37.3(a)(2): an owner who refrains from imposing an annual increase 'may accumulate said increase and, subject to Section 37.15, impose that amount on the tenant's subsequent rent increase anniversary dates.' No 24-month condition appears.

finding: Rule 4.12 timing condition
verified_value: 'A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable.'

finding: sf.gov banking page wording
verified_value: 'A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase.'
note: Quoted as published. It cannot be reconciled with Rule 4.12 or with the Board's own worked examples; see the next two rows.

finding: Official worked examples test the threshold from both sides
verified_value: Example 1: a 1.7% increase available 6/1/2024 is banked when the increase is imposed 5/1/2026 (23 months). Example 2: a 1.4% increase available 6/1/2025 is not banked and is permanently lost when the increase is imposed 5/1/2026 (11 months). Example 3: the banking page itself treats a 1.7% increase available 8/1/2024 as banked on 8/1/2025 (12 months). Every example applies a 12-month test measured from the date the increase became available.

finding: Can the 24-month sentence be reconciled with those examples?
verified_value: No. The examples bank an increase 12 months after it became available and lose one after 11 months. A 24-month requirement would exclude both. Rule 4.12 therefore states the controlling test, and the 24-month sentence is an unresolved inconsistency on the guidance page.
note: Interpretation, not a quoted rule. Published as F04. Rule 4.12 is the test applied to both units; the arithmetic is conditional on the unverified rent history described in F01 and F18.

finding: Does the 24-month wording change these two units' figures?
verified_value: It could, which is why it is flagged. Under Rule 4.12 (12 months from availability), and assuming no intervening increases, Unit 1 reaches 3.0% and Unit 2 13.1%. Applied literally to each increase, the 24-month sentence would cut Unit 1 to 1.6% ($63.92) and Unit 2 to 11.7% ($368.55). The annual-only options are unaffected either way.
note: The banked options therefore carry a confirmation step with a Rent Board counsellor before service.

finding: Compounding and rounding of banked amounts
verified_value: Banked increases are added, not compounded, and may not be rounded up. An administrative law judge may readjust a good-faith overage of no more than one-half of one percent.

finding: Notice content for a banked increase
verified_value: State which portion is banked and the dates it is based on. Rule 4.12(b) says failure to include this does not by itself render the increase null and void.

finding: Does a banked amount survive a new tenancy?
verified_value: No. Banked increases do not carry over to a new tenant. A new owner may use a prior owner's bank.

finding: Changing the anniversary date
verified_value: Moving the effective date off the anniversary can permanently lose an increase that has not yet completed its 12 months. Many owners keep the same date each year to avoid this.

finding: Notice period, increase of 10% or less
verified_value: At least 30 days before the effective date.

finding: Notice period, increase above 10%
verified_value: At least 90 days before the effective date.

finding: How the 10% threshold is measured
verified_value: Against the rent charged at any time in the 12 months before the effective date, alone or combined with any other increases in that 12-month window.

finding: Extra time when serving by mail
verified_value: Add 5 days.

finding: Permitted methods of service
verified_value: Personal delivery to the tenant, or mail under Code of Civil Procedure sec. 1013.

finding: Required notice content
verified_value: Dollar amount, percentage amount, effective date, and which portion is banked.

finding: Consequence of a defective notice
verified_value: Rule 4.10(b): a non-conforming increase is null and void in its entirety, subject only to a good-faith readjustment where the excess is no more than one-half of one percent.

finding: Must the notice state a reason?
verified_value: No reason is required for an annual or banked increase; the ordinance itself authorises it. Reasons and cost proof attach to petition-based increases.

finding: Which units are rent controlled
verified_value: Many residential units built on or before June 13, 1979 have rent control and eviction protection.

finding: Does the statewide cap apply to these units?
verified_value: No. AB 1482's rent cap does not apply to housing already under a local rent control ordinance that restricts increases below the state formula.

finding: Statewide cap figure (reference only)
verified_value: 8.8% for San Francisco, 8/1/2026 - 7/31/2027 (5% + 3.8% CPI). Does not govern these units.

finding: Two-unit owner-occupied exemption under AB 1482
verified_value: A two-unit property is exempt only if the second unit was owner-occupied for the entire tenancy. Both units here are tenant-occupied, so this exemption is not available.

finding: Federal ceiling on rent increases
note: No federal statute capping rent increases for private, unsubsidised housing was identified in the sources reviewed. Federal housing law in this area is anti-discrimination law.

finding: Federal protected classes
verified_value: Race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability.

finding: California protected classes (broader than federal)
verified_value: Adds ancestry, citizenship, immigration status, primary language, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, genetic information, marital status, source of income, military or veteran status, and age.

finding: Retaliation
verified_value: Civil Code sec. 1942.5 bars a rent increase within 180 days of specified tenant activity such as a habitability complaint; sec. 1942.5(d) separately prohibits retaliatory increases without that time limit.

finding: Bad-faith increases used to force a tenant out
verified_value: Sec. 37.10B(a)(5) prohibits influencing a tenant to vacate by fraud, intimidation or coercion; (a)(9) prohibits violating anti-discrimination law. Treble damages or $1,000 minimum, plus fees.

finding: Algorithmic rent-setting software
verified_value: Sec. 37.10C makes it unlawful to use revenue-management software that draws on non-public competitor data to set rents. Each month and each unit is a separate violation.

finding: Must both units be raised to avoid discrimination?
note: No provision requiring identical or simultaneous increases across units was found. What is prohibited is a difference based on a protected characteristic, or a retaliatory/bad-faith purpose.

finding: Do corporations and individual owners face different caps?
verified_value: No. Sec. 37.3 applies to 'landlords' without distinguishing entity form; the same 1.6% governs both.

finding: What large operators may not do here
verified_value: Use algorithmic revenue-management devices built on non-public competitor data - unlawful in San Francisco for any landlord, corporate or individual.

finding: Charging more because a roommate moved in
verified_value: Unlawful. An owner cannot charge additional rent simply because a new or additional roommate moved in with the existing tenant, even if the lease says otherwise.

finding: Rule 6.14 notice on a new occupant
verified_value: To preserve an unlimited increase when the last original occupant vacates, a written 6.14 notice must be served on each subsequent occupant within a reasonable time; generally 60 days is considered reasonable.

finding: Costa-Hawkins and co-tenants
verified_value: A co-tenant who moved in after the original occupant is not subject to a Costa-Hawkins increase. Rule 6.14 is broader but requires the timely notice.

finding: Tenant challenge route
verified_value: Tenant Petition Form 516C, box C, alleging an unlawful rent increase. No filing charge and no time limit for filing.

finding: What the tenant will be asked to produce
verified_value: Original lease, rent increase notices, rent receipts or cancelled checks showing the date and amount of increases.
note: Keep the same evidence file. It is the answer to most of the questions a tenant lawyer will ask.

finding: Free counsel
verified_value: The Tenant Right to Counsel Program provides free assistance in eviction cases; intake is through the Eviction Defense Collaborative, (415) 659-9184.
note: This is eviction defence, not a free lawyer for every rent increase dispute.

finding: Free Rent Board counselling
verified_value: Rent Board counsellors, 415-252-4600, weekdays 9am-noon and 1pm-4pm. Available to owners as well as tenants.

finding: Hearing format
verified_value: Designed so that no one needs an attorney; parties may still be represented. The judge cannot consider evidence outside the record or not served on the other side.
